topic: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
title: Human rights and international policy
blurb: Link everyday learning disability care to the Human Rights Act articles and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.
question: Mia, 31, has a learning disability and lives in a care home arranged and paid for by the council. Staff routinely open and read her personal letters before giving them to her. Which right is most directly engaged, and does the Human Rights Act apply to this privately run home?

teach.body: The Human Rights Act 1998 brings the European Convention rights into UK law. Under section 6 it is unlawful for a public authority, such as an NHS trust or council, to act in a way that is incompatible with a Convention right. People with a learning disability have the same rights as anyone else. In plain English: every restriction, routine and decision in care must respect the person's rights, and staff must be able to justify any interference.

teach.h: Five articles in learning disability care
head: Article
Right
LD care example
rows: Delayed treatment of sepsis or pneumonia
No torture, inhuman or degrading treatment
Left in soiled bedding for hours
Private and family life, home, correspondence
No discrimination in enjoying the rights

teach.caption: Article 8(2): interference must be in accordance with the law and necessary in a democratic society for a listed aim.

teach.h: Private providers can be covered too
teach.body: A registered care provider in England that provides personal care or residential care arranged or paid for by a local authority is treated as exercising a function of a public nature under the Human Rights Act. So a privately owned care home or home care agency delivering council-arranged care must respect Convention rights in the same way as a public body.

Mia, 31, lives in a privately run care home arranged by the council. Staff open her letters 'to check for anything upsetting'. This interferes with Article 8 (correspondence and private life), and the Human Rights Act applies because her care is council-arranged (Care Act s73). The nurse raises it with the manager, makes sure Mia receives her post unopened, offers support to read letters if she wants it, and records her preferences in her care plan.

teach.h: The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities

items.label: Adopted by the UN General Assembly

teach.caption: The UK also ratified the Optional Protocol, allowing individual complaints to the UN committee once UK remedies are exhausted.

head: Article
Right
In practice
rows: Choice of where and with whom to live
Respect for home and the family
Same quality of care; free, informed consent
teach.caption: Article 3 sets the general principles, including dignity, autonomy, non-discrimination and inclusion.

teach.h: How the CRPD works in the UK
teach.body: The CRPD is an international treaty. It is not directly enforceable in UK courts, so a person cannot sue simply for breach of it. It still matters: it shapes policy, guides how UK law such as the Equality Act is interpreted, and sets the standard services are measured against. In practice, rights are enforced through the Human Rights Act, the Equality Act and the Mental Capacity Act.

items: Question blanket rules (bedtimes, phones, visitors): each restriction must be individual and justified.
Support the person to make their own choices and to communicate them.
Offer or refer for advocacy when a person's voice is not being heard.
Challenge and report degrading or discriminatory care at once.

teach.text: Article 14 is not a free-standing right: it protects against discrimination in the enjoyment of the other Convention rights, so it is used alongside another article such as Article 8 or Article 2. And do not treat the CRPD as directly enforceable in a UK court: it guides interpretation and policy.

items: HRA s6: public authorities must act compatibly with Convention rights.
Care Act s73: registered providers of council-arranged care count as public for HRA purposes.
Articles 2, 3, 5, 8 and 14 map onto everyday LD care; Article 3 is absolute, Article 8 is qualified.
CRPD: UK ratified 8 June 2009; Articles 12, 19, 23 and 25; not directly enforceable in UK courts.
Challenge blanket rules, support choice and use advocacy.

summary: You can now match learning disability care situations to the Human Rights Act articles, tell absolute from qualified rights, and explain when private providers are covered. You can also describe the UN CRPD, its key articles and its status in UK law.

A.q: Mia, 31, has a learning disability and lives in a care home. Staff routinely open and read her personal letters before handing them to her. Which Convention right is most directly engaged?
options: Article 5, the right to liberty and security
Article 3, freedom from degrading treatment
Article 14, the prohibition of discrimination
Article 8, respect for private life and correspondence
A.why: Article 8 protects respect for private and family life, home and correspondence. Reading her letters interferes with it.

whyNot.0: Article 5 concerns deprivation of liberty, not privacy of letters.
whyNot.1: Opening letters is an intrusion on privacy; Article 3 concerns treatment severe enough to be inhuman or degrading.
whyNot.2: Article 14 is used with another right and is not the right most directly engaged here.

A.q: During an unannounced visit, a nurse finds that Mark, 45, who has a profound learning disability, has been left in soiled bedding for many hours while staff watched television. Which right is most directly engaged?
options: Article 2, the right to life of every person
Article 3, freedom from inhuman or degrading treatment
Article 5, the right to liberty and security
Article 9, freedom of thought, conscience and religion
A.why: Leaving a dependent person in soiled bedding for hours can be degrading treatment, engaging Article 3, which is absolute.

whyNot.0: Article 2 is engaged when life is at risk; the core issue here is degrading treatment.
whyNot.2: Article 5 concerns deprivation of liberty, not standards of personal care.
whyNot.3: Article 9 concerns thought, conscience and religion.

A.q: A learning disability nurse is preparing a teaching session on the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Which statement about its status in the UK is correct?
options: It was ratified in 2009 and guides how UK law is interpreted
It was made part of UK law by the Human Rights Act 1998
It can be enforced directly by claims in UK county courts
It applies to the NHS but not to local authority services
A.why: The UK ratified the CRPD on 8 June 2009. It is not directly enforceable in UK courts but shapes policy and the interpretation of UK law.

whyNot.1: The HRA incorporates the European Convention on Human Rights, not the CRPD, which came later.
whyNot.2: The CRPD is not directly enforceable in UK courts.
whyNot.3: The CRPD binds the state as a whole, not one service sector.

B.q: Ken, 56, has a learning disability and lives in a privately owned care home. His place is arranged and paid for by the local authority. His sister asks whether the Human Rights Act applies to the home's care of Ken. What is the correct answer?
options: No, the Act applies to NHS bodies and not to care homes
No, a private company is outside the Act in every case
Yes, council-arranged care is treated as a public function
Yes, but because Ken's sister has asked for it to apply
B.why: Care Act 2014 s73: a registered provider giving residential care arranged or paid for by a local authority is treated as exercising a public function under HRA s6(3)(b).

whyNot.0: The Act covers public authorities generally, and s73 brings council-arranged care homes within it.
whyNot.1: Private providers can be covered when performing public functions, as s73 makes clear.
whyNot.3: The Act's application does not depend on a relative's request.

B.q: A student asks how Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights can be relied on by a person with a learning disability. What is the best answer?
options: It is a free-standing right to equal treatment in all areas
It is used with another Convention right, such as Article 8
It can be used for employment claims in a tribunal
It applies to private shops and restaurants directly
B.why: Article 14 secures the enjoyment of the Convention rights without discrimination, so it is relied on together with another article.

whyNot.0: Article 14 is not free-standing; it attaches to the other Convention rights.
whyNot.2: Employment discrimination claims are brought under the Equality Act 2010.
whyNot.3: HRA duties fall on public authorities; private shops are covered by the Equality Act.

B.q: A council-funded supported living service wants to restrict how often Paul, 37, who has a learning disability and capacity, can see his partner. Under Article 8, when could such an interference be lawful?
options: When his family support the restriction in writing
When it is set out in the service's house rules
When staffing levels make visits hard to supervise
When lawful, necessary and proportionate to a legitimate aim
B.why: Article 8 is qualified: interference must be in accordance with the law and necessary for a legitimate aim such as protecting health or the rights of others, and proportionate.

whyNot.0: Family support does not make an interference with an adult's private life lawful.
whyNot.1: A house rule is not a lawful justification by itself and suggests a blanket approach.
whyNot.2: Staffing convenience is not a legitimate aim under Article 8(2).

C.q: In a council-funded group home, all residents must hand in their mobile phones at 9pm. Shona, 29, has a learning disability and capacity, and is upset because she calls her mother at night. What is the most appropriate action for the visiting nurse?
options: Challenge the blanket rule and support Shona to access advocacy
Explain that house rules apply equally to all residents
Ask her mother to call earlier so that the rule is kept
Suggest Shona uses the staff phone under supervision
C.why: A blanket rule interferes with Article 8 without individual justification. The nurse should challenge it and help Shona have her voice heard, including through advocacy.

whyNot.1: Applying a rule to everyone does not justify interfering with each person's private life.
whyNot.2: This works around the rule instead of addressing the unjustified restriction.
whyNot.3: Supervised calls are a further interference with her privacy, not a solution.

C.q: Rafi, 40, has a learning disability and has lived on a hospital ward for six years. He says he wants his own flat near his brother. Which CRPD article most directly supports his wish?
options: Article 12, equal recognition before the law
Article 25, the right to health
Article 19, living independently in the community
Article 23, respect for home and the family
C.why: CRPD Article 19 recognises the equal right to live in the community, including choosing where and with whom to live, and not being obliged to live in a particular arrangement.

whyNot.0: Article 12 concerns legal capacity and recognition as a person before the law.
whyNot.1: Article 25 concerns access to health care of the same quality as others.
whyNot.3: Article 23 concerns marriage, family, parenthood and relationships.

C.q: A consultant suggests not offering Ella, 52, who has a learning disability, the same cancer screening as other women 'as it will distress her'. Which CRPD article most directly requires health professionals to provide care of the same quality to her?
options: Article 19, living independently
Article 25, health
Article 12, equal recognition before the law
Article 23, respect for home and family
C.why: CRPD Article 25 requires the same range and quality of health care, including population-based public health programmes, and care of the same quality based on free and informed consent.

whyNot.0: Article 19 concerns where and with whom a person lives.
whyNot.2: Article 12 concerns legal capacity, not the quality of health care.
whyNot.3: Article 23 concerns family life and relationships.

reteach.title: Match the care problem to the right
reteach.question: When you see a problem in care, how do you name the right that is at stake?

blocks.h: Ask what is being taken away
blocks.body: Is life at risk? Article 2. Is the person being degraded? Article 3, which can never be justified. Is their freedom restricted? Article 5. Is their privacy, home, family or post being interfered with? Article 8. Are they treated differently in any of these because of their disability? Add Article 14.

blocks.text: The CRPD sets the standard but is not directly enforceable in UK courts; the HRA, Equality Act and MCA are the routes in practice.

explain.body: HRA s6: public authorities, including NHS trusts and councils, must act compatibly with Convention rights. Care Act s73 extends this to registered providers giving council-arranged personal or residential care.

test.q: Which body must act compatibly with Convention rights under section 6 of the Human Rights Act?
options: A private dental practice
An NHS trust
A self-funded hairdresser
A family carer at home
test.why: An NHS trust is a public authority under HRA s6.

whyNot.0: A purely private practice is not a public authority for this purpose.
whyNot.2: A private business serving the public is covered by the Equality Act, not s6 of the HRA.
whyNot.3: A family carer is not a public authority.

explain.body: Article 2 life; 3 inhuman or degrading treatment; 5 liberty; 8 private and family life, home and correspondence; 14 discrimination in the enjoyment of those rights.

test.q: A residential home stops Jo, 27, who has a learning disability and capacity, from seeing her boyfriend because staff disapprove of the relationship. Which right is most directly engaged?
options: Article 2
Article 3
Article 8
Article 5
test.why: Article 8 protects private and family life, which includes relationships.

whyNot.0: Article 2 concerns the right to life.
whyNot.1: Article 3 concerns torture and inhuman or degrading treatment.
whyNot.3: Article 5 concerns deprivation of liberty, not choice of relationships.

explain.body: Article 3 is absolute: no justification can make degrading treatment lawful. Article 8 is qualified: it can be interfered with if lawful, necessary and proportionate for a legitimate aim such as health or the rights of others.

test.q: Which Convention right is absolute, so that no interference with it can be justified?
options: Article 8, private and family life
Article 5, liberty
Article 10, freedom of expression
Article 3, degrading treatment
test.why: Article 3 contains no exceptions: no one shall be subjected to torture or inhuman or degrading treatment.

whyNot.1: Article 5 lists lawful grounds for detention.
whyNot.2: Article 10 is qualified: Article 10(2) allows restrictions prescribed by law and necessary in a democratic society.

explain.body: Adopted 2006; UK ratified 8 June 2009. Key articles: 12 equal recognition before the law, 19 living independently, 23 home and family, 25 health. Not directly enforceable in UK courts, but it guides interpretation and policy.

test.q: Which CRPD article addresses the rights of disabled people to marriage, parenthood and family life?
options: Article 23
Article 19
Article 25
Article 12
test.why: CRPD Article 23 (respect for home and the family) covers marriage, family, parenthood and relationships.

whyNot.1: Article 19 covers living independently in the community.
whyNot.3: Article 12 covers equal recognition before the law.
